query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during high‐temperature sliding of a FeNiCrCoCu coating are governed by the formation of a continuous, adherent oxide layer at the sliding interface. This oxide scale—primarily rich in Cr-derived oxides—acts as a barrier that reduces metal-metal contact, limits dislocation nucleation and mobility, and thereby mitigates localized plastic deformation and abrasive wear.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy thin coating on a conventional metal substrate in the as-deposited, unoxidized state
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled pre-oxidation treatment designed to develop a uniform, nano-scale oxide layer on the coating surface before high-temperature sliding tests
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding regime (e.g., around 600–700 °C) in a controlled atmosphere that permits oxidation kinetics
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, nanocrystalline oxide layer (predominantly Cr oxide) that forms at the surface and sliding interface
generation.mechanism: The pre-formed oxide layer protects the metallic coating by impeding direct asperity contact, thereby reducing stress concentrations and limiting the initiation of dislocation motion and shear band formation during sliding. This barrier effect results in lower local plastic deformation and reduced wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline (unoxidized coating), the pre-oxidized coating should exhibit lower wear rates and reduced microscopic plastic deformation under high-temperature sliding conditions.
generation.baseline: FeNiCrCoCu coating without the pre-oxidation treatment—i.e., an as-deposited, unoxidized coating
generation.boundary: This protective mechanism is expected to be effective primarily in high-temperature regimes (≥600 °C) where oxidation kinetics are sufficiently active; at lower temperatures, the oxide scale may not form consistently, limiting the effect.
generation.uncertainty: The precise oxide composition, optimal thickness, and uniformity needed for maximum protection remain uncertain, as does the minimum temperature threshold required to develop the beneficial oxide scale.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical FeNiCrCoCu coatings on conventional metal substrates. Subject one set to a controlled pre-oxidation treatment to develop a continuous oxide layer, while leaving the other set in the as-deposited state. Perform high-temperature sliding wear tests at approximately 650 °C under identical mechanical and atmospheric conditions.
measurements: Quantitative wear rate (e.g., mass loss, wear track depth)
Microscopic characterization of deformation features via SEM/TEM (to assess dislocation structures and shear band formation)
Surface and cross-sectional analysis of the oxide layer (using XPS/EDS) to verify its continuity and composition
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized coatings do not show a statistically significant reduction in wear rate and microscopic plastic deformation compared to the untreated coatings under controlled high-temperature sliding conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.
